summary: First English narrative for Harold II's decision in October 1066 to move against William of Normandy before the full English host had gathered, written from the case's verified facts (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, Ingram translation; English Heritage). Later traditions (the Gyrth/Gytha plea, the 200-mile forced march) are identified as such.

narrative.hook: Two weeks after crushing a Norwegian army in the north, the King of England is back in London, and a second invader has dug in on the Sussex coast. Fresh troops are trickling in. Do you march on William now, or wait until the whole kingdom has gathered?
narrative.short_setup: It is October 1066. Harold Godwinson has been king since January. All summer a great English army and fleet waited on the south coast for William of Normandy, until early September, when the food ran out and the men had to be sent home. Then the threat came from the other direction: Harald Hardrada of Norway, joined by Harold's own brother Tostig, landed in the north and beat the northern earls near York on 20 September. Harold rode north day and night and on 25 September caught the invaders off guard at Stamford Bridge, where both Hardrada and Tostig were killed, though many English died too. Three days later William landed at Pevensey and built a castle at Hastings, in Sussex, where Harold's own family lands lay. The news probably reached Harold around 2 October. Now in London, the king is raising new forces from the southern counties and must decide when to move.
narrative.why_option_a_made_sense: Speed had just won a war. At Stamford Bridge Harold came on the Norwegians before they expected the English and destroyed them. William, too, was still close to the landing beach, and every day the Normans were left alone was a day to strengthen their castle and their grip on the coast. That coast was the king's own family country, and a king who sat in London while an invader held it would look weak to the people whose loyalty a new reign depended on. And the summer had taught a hard lesson: an English army, once gathered, could not be kept in the field for ever. Waiting for the whole host risked watching it shrink again.
narrative.why_option_b_made_sense: Harold's men had fought one hard battle and covered the length of the country in a few weeks; many of them were dead or worn out. The northern earls' forces had been beaten at Fulford. The new troops from the south were only beginning to arrive, and the fleet that might have threatened William's ships had been scattered and partly lost in September. An invader on the coast was not going anywhere quickly either. Time to rest the veterans and draw in more men from across the kingdom would let Harold face William with the largest army England could raise, rather than whatever could be collected in a few days.
narrative.actual_decision_explanation: Harold moved quickly. The English sources say the king left London before the full strength of the army had gathered. No contemporary source records the reasons, so any account of them is reconstruction. Some chroniclers say Harold spent several days in London, up to six in one account, raising men from the southern shires. Writers a century later told of Harold's mother Gytha and brother Gyrth urging delay and being angrily refused, but that story does not appear in the contemporary chronicle and should be read as later tradition. The old picture of a desperate 200-mile forced march south is not in the contemporary sources either.
narrative.outcome_story: On 14 October 1066, the day of Pope Calixtus, the armies met near Hastings. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says William came upon the king before the English army was collected, and that Harold fought with the men who would stand by the king. There was great slaughter on both sides. Harold was killed, with two brothers, Leofwine and Gyrth, and the Normans held the field. The English leaders in London talked of making the young Edgar the Ætheling king, and the earls Edwin and Morcar promised to fight, but, as the chronicler put it, the more urgent the business, the later and worse it went from day to day. William ravaged the country as the Norman army advanced. At Berkhamsted the archbishop, Edgar, the earls and the leading men of London submitted, and on Christmas Day 1066 William was consecrated king at Westminster.
narrative.hindsight_analysis:
Because Harold lost, it is easy to say the decision to move fast was rash. Because Harold had just won by moving fast, it is just as easy to call it bold. The evidence supports neither verdict with confidence.

On decision quality, this case is rated unclear. The reasons for speed were real: a strengthening enemy on the coast, the king's own lands at stake, a recent victory won by surprise, and the hard summer lesson that armies dissolve. The reasons for waiting were also real: tired and depleted veterans, a beaten northern levy, reinforcements only starting to arrive. What would decide the question is what waiting would actually have produced, how many more men and how soon, and the sources do not tell us. They do not even record how large either army was, or what Harold was thinking. A decision should be judged on what its maker could know; here even that is largely lost.

On outcome quality, the result was as bad as it could be for Harold and for English rule: the king and two brothers dead, the army broken, and a kingdom that submitted within weeks. But the outcome of a single battle carries a great deal of chance. The Chronicle itself saw the fight as hard-fought on both sides. The same decision, made the same way, might have produced a different result on a different day.

It is also worth noticing how the story of this decision has changed. Two of its most vivid details, the exhausting forced march and the brother's plea for delay, come from later tradition rather than from the contemporary record. Hindsight did not only judge the decision; it helped write it.
narrative.decision_principle: When the most important facts about the alternative (how much stronger waiting would really make you) are unknown, a defeat does not prove that acting fast was wrong, and a recent success does not prove that it was right.
narrative.longform_story:
England had a new king in 1066. When Edward the Confessor died in early January, Harold Godwinson was crowned at Westminster. Harold knew the crown would be challenged. Across the Channel, Duke William of Normandy claimed it too.

All that summer Harold prepared. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says the king gathered a land and sea force larger than any king had raised before. It took a long time to collect the fleet, and when it was ready the king took it to the Isle of Wight, while soldiers watched the coast. They waited all summer and into the harvest. William did not come. By the Nativity of St Mary, 8 September, the provisions were gone and no one could hold the men any longer. They were sent home. The ships were brought round to London, and many were lost on the way.

The invasion came from the north instead. King Harald Hardrada of Norway, with Harold's brother Tostig, sailed up the Ouse towards York. On 20 September the northern earls, Edwin and Morcar, met the invaders and were beaten after great slaughter. Harold went north day and night, gathering men as the army went, and on 25 September came upon the Norwegians unawares at Stamford Bridge. The fighting lasted long into the day. Hardrada and Tostig were killed, and the surviving Norwegians were allowed to sail home. Two great battles had been fought within five nights.

Three days later, on the eve of Michaelmas, William landed at Pevensey on the Sussex coast and soon built a castle at Hastings. The news probably reached Harold, still in the north, around 2 October. By some accounts the king then spent several days in London, up to six in one telling, raising new forces from the southern counties. Sussex was home ground for Harold's family. An invader was now settled there.

This was the decision. Should the king march at once, with the men who had come through Stamford Bridge and whatever the south could send in a few days? Or should the army wait in London until the whole strength of the kingdom had gathered?

There was a strong case for speed. Surprise had just destroyed one invader. William was still close to the landing beach, building defences; given time, the Normans would only grow stronger. The coast being held was the king's own, and a king newly crowned could not afford to look as though invaders could do as they pleased. And the summer had shown what happened to an English army kept waiting: it ran out of food and went home.

There was a strong case for waiting too. The men who had marched north and fought at Stamford Bridge were tired, and many were dead. The northern levies had been mauled at Fulford. Fresh men from the southern shires were only beginning to arrive. The fleet was scattered and damaged. William, on the coast, was not going anywhere fast. Days spent gathering might mean meeting the Normans with a much larger army.

What Harold weighed, no contemporary source tells us. What Harold did is clearer. The English sources agree that the king moved before the whole army had come in. A century later, writers told how Harold's mother Gytha and brother Gyrth begged for delay, and how the king angrily refused. It is a powerful scene, but it is not in the Chronicle, and it may say more about how later generations understood the defeat than about what was said in London. The famous image of an exhausted army force-marching 200 miles south is also absent from the contemporary sources. One modern historian has suggested that some of the men may have come south by ship.

On 14 October, the day of Pope Calixtus, the armies met near Hastings. The Chronicle's account is short and grim. William came against the king before the English army was gathered, and the king fought with the men who would stand by the crown. There was great slaughter on both sides. Harold was killed, with two brothers, Leofwine and Gyrth. The French held the field, 'as God granted them for the sins of the nation', the chronicler wrote.

What followed was a slow collapse. In London, Archbishop Ealdred and the citizens wanted to make the young Edgar the Ætheling king, and the earls Edwin and Morcar promised to fight. But nothing came of it. The more urgent things became, the chronicler lamented, the later and worse it went from day to day. William ravaged the country as the Normans advanced, and at Berkhamsted the English leaders came out and submitted. On Christmas Day William was crowned at Westminster.

Was Harold rash? It is the obvious verdict, and it may be wrong. The case for speed was real, and the same instinct had won Stamford Bridge only weeks before. The case for waiting was real too. What would settle it is knowledge we do not have: how large the armies were, how many more men waiting would have brought, and how quickly. A single battle also turns on things no one can plan. The fairest conclusion is that the decision cannot be graded with confidence on the evidence that survives. The defeat was certain. Whether the choice behind it was a mistake is not.
